prose: A READ OF THE SURVIVING CANON SET FOR CLAIMS ABOUT TOOL BEHAVIOUR -- a flag, an exit code, a spelling, a default -- ASKING OF EACH WHETHER THE TOOL ITSELF ANSWERS THE SAME QUESTION. Where it does, the document must point at the answering verb rather than restate the answer. NON-TEST BECAUSE THE JUDGEMENT IS WHETHER A SENTENCE IS A CLAIM ABOUT THE BUILD AT ALL, which is a reading, not a pattern: "run `intent upgrade` to convert" is a claim about a verb existing, "`--skip-settings` was not carried into v3" is a claim about a build, and no grep separates them. THE READ IS AGAINST A NAMED BUILD AND SAYS WHICH, because a claim about the tool is a claim about a REVISION and this estate is a port -- a v2-true sentence reads identically after it stops being true of v3, and a re-drive aimed at its CITATION passes. WHAT MAKES A SURVIVING CLAIM ACCEPTABLE IS NOT THAT IT IS CURRENTLY TRUE: it is that something other than a human's memory will notice when it stops being.
note: NOT YET DONE, and it needs a BUILD named at the time of the read rather than a date. The WP-01 catalogue measured against `intent 3.0.0 (4479264f)` on 2026-08-28, with a scratch `intent init` in an empty directory as its control -- which is the right shape -- but that build is many commits behind and the surviving set has not been cut yet. THIS NOTE WAS WRITTEN TWICE: the first attempt passed it as an inline double-quoted shell argument, and zsh executed every backticked span in it as a command. Both citations were replaced with nothing, the row was created, and the tool printed `ok`. The note read plausibly and had silently lost the two facts it existed to carry.
